transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, doctor, it's... it's a lot, honestly. I wasn't even sure I should come in, but my husband kept telling me I needed to talk to somebody, and I guess he's right because I'm just so terrified lately. I work down at the distribution warehouse—I'm an order filler, have been for a long time, so I'm used to it being loud and busy, you know? You've got pallets dropping, beeping forklifts, people yelling across the aisles all shift long. You get used to the noise. But this wasn't that. 

What really scared me enough to finally make this appointment and actually sit in this chair today is... well, I've been hearing my name. And not just, you know, thinking I heard it in the wind or something. I'll be at home, just trying to relax, and I'll hear my name called clear as day from the hallway. I'll get up and look, and nobody is there. Just an empty hallway. And then it happened at work, too, which really shook me up. I was in the back aisle at the warehouse pulling some stock, completely alone in that section, and I heard it again. It wasn't over the intercom or a coworker messing with me. It sounded... I mean, it sounds as real and as close as my husband standing right next to me speaking right into my ear. I spun right around expecting my supervisor or someone to be right there, but there was absolutely no one. Just empty shelves. It's just so real, every single time, and it's driving me crazy trying to figure out where it's coming from. I just... I don't know what's happening.
Have you seen or felt anything unusual that isn't really there, like shadows or voices is one thing, but maybe smells, tastes, or things you see?

No, doctor, no... I haven't had anything like that happen. I mean, I've been paying real close attention to everything lately, because once you start hearing your name when nobody's around, you really start second-guessing your own mind, you know? Like, just the other day my husband was cooking breakfast—he makes this awful turkey bacon because he's trying to watch his cholesterol—and I smelled it from the bedroom and for a split second I actually panicked. I thought, 'Oh my lord, is the bacon even real or am I making that up too?' But I went out there and he was right there at the stove, plain as day. So, no, no weird smells or tastes. 

And I haven't seen anything either, no shadows or ghosts or whatever. The warehouse can get pretty dark in the back sections, especially near the loading docks where the fluorescent lights are always buzzing and flickering—management has been saying they'd replace those bulbs for six months now, I swear, they never get around to maintenance—but even in that bad lighting, I never see anything that isn't supposed to be there. Just the racks and the boxes and the dust. And nobody's touching me or anything like that, no weird feelings on my skin. 

It's really just the hearing part. Just my name. Which is plenty, honestly, because it just throws my whole day off. I'll be looking around for whoever said it, expecting to see a person, but my eyes are telling me the truth. There's never anybody there. It's just the sound that's playing tricks on me, nothing else.
Do you hear your name being called all the time, or does it happen at specific times or intervals?

Well, no, it's not all the time, thank goodness, because I don't think I could survive if it was every single minute of the day. It's actually... well, it's really specific when it happens. Looking back on it now, it really only started up during that... that really intense stretch I had a little while ago. 

You see, for about a week or so, I was just... I was completely wired. I don't even know how else to explain it. I was barely sleeping, maybe an hour or two a night, if that, but I wasn't tired at all. I was practically buzzing. I was talking a mile a minute, just non-stop, telling my husband about all these grand plans I had to reorganize the entire garage, the basement, the attic—which we don't even use—and I just felt this overwhelming, intense drive to fix absolutely everything in the house. I was painting the trim in the living room at three in the morning, and I was so sure I was doing the most important work of my life. 

And that's... that's exactly when I started hearing it. While I was in the middle of all that endless energy, that's when my name started being called from the hallway or at the warehouse. It was during that exact time. But before that? Never. I'd never heard a thing out of the ordinary in my forty-eight years on this earth. And then, well, after that high-energy phase kind of crashed, and I fell into this really awful, dark, withdrawn period where I couldn't even get out of bed to face the day... the voice stopped. I haven't heard it since I got so low and quiet. It's like it only existed when my brain was running at a hundred miles an hour, and once I shut down, the voice shut down too. So, no, it's not all the time, just... just during that one really wild stretch.
During that week when you were barely sleeping and had all that energy, did you feel like you were on top of the world, invincible, or unusually confident?

Well, yes, actually. It's funny you use that exact phrase, on top of the world, because that is exactly... I mean, that is exactly how it felt. I felt like I couldn't make a mistake if I tried, which is so unlike me. Usually, I'm just, you know, punching the clock at the warehouse, putting my head down, doing my job, paying the bills. But that week... oh my lord, I was just bursting with these huge, incredible ideas. 

I do a little bit of crafting on the side, mostly resin work, like coasters and little decorative trays with dried flowers in them, and some knitting when my hands aren't too cramped up from pulling stock all shift. Usually it's just a hobby, just for me or for birthday gifts for my nieces, nothing serious. But right then, during that stretch where I wasn't sleeping and had all that energy? I got it in my head that I was an absolute genius. I was completely convinced that I could turn my crafts into a real retirement business, and not just eventually, but right away. 

I remember I was sitting at the kitchen table at maybe three or four in the morning, just buzzing, writing out this massive, elaborate business plan on the back of our electric bills and grocery receipts. I was talking a mile a minute to my husband—who was just standing there in his pajamas begging me to please just come to bed—telling him that I was going to quit the warehouse, open a fancy storefront downtown, and that we were going to be practically rich overnight. I just knew it in my bones. I felt so incredibly smart, like everyone would see I had figured out the perfect plan for our family. I honestly thought people would be lining up down the block for my little resin coasters and that I was about to be some famous entrepreneur. Looking back on it now, it's a little embarrassing because I'm not a business person, I'm an order filler, but in that moment, I really believed I was untouchable and that I had all the answers to everything.
Did you make any impulsive decisions or purchases during that week when you had all the energy and felt invincible?

Well, no, surprisingly. I mean, I really, really wanted to, don't get me wrong. I had my laptop open on the kitchen counter—right next to all those electric bills and receipts I was writing my master plan on—and I must have had about fifty different tabs open on the browser. 

I was looking at bulk suppliers for epoxy resin, you know, the industrial two-part kind that you have to mix perfectly or it gets all cloudy and ruins the whole batch? I had my online shopping cart just completely loaded up. I'm talking gallons of the stuff, plus all these intricate silicone molds, the big ones for making tiered cake stands and serving trays, and enough gold leaf and mica powder to cover the entire warehouse floor where I work. I was ready to drop at least two thousand dollars right then and there. I had the credit card out of my purse and everything.

But... well, my husband, he's a very practical man, and he saw what I was doing. He actually came over, put his hand over mine, and gently closed the laptop screen. Oh, I was so mad at him in that moment! I really was. I told him he was stifling my creativity, that he just didn't have the vision, and that he was ruining our one big chance at early retirement. We bickered about it for a good hour while he was just trying to get me to drink a glass of water and go to sleep. But honestly, thank goodness for him, because I never actually clicked 'checkout' on any of it. 

And as for decisions, like I said before, I *told* him I was going to quit my job. I fully intended to march into the supervisor's office first thing Monday morning—Gary is his name, he's been the floor manager for twelve years and he's a real stickler for attendance, always breathing down our necks about scan rates—and I was going to march right in there, slam my safety vest on his desk, and tell him I was moving on to bigger and better things. 

But by the time Monday actually rolled around, that intense energy had already started to sort of... leak out of me, I guess. I was still feeling restless, but the grand ideas were fading, and I didn't actually go through with it. I just put my vest on and clocked in like normal, even though I was starting to feel completely exhausted from not sleeping. So, no, I didn't actually spend our savings or throw away my job, thank heavens. I just made a whole lot of noise about doing it. I really think if that phase had lasted even one more day, though, I would have drained the joint checking account on craft supplies we have absolutely no room for. But no, no real damage done, just a lot of talk.
When you fell into that really awful, dark, withdrawn period after your energy crashed, did you feel sad or hopeless most of the time?

Well, yes. Honestly, sad almost feels like too small of a word for it, if that makes sense. After all that running around and arguing with my husband over the laptop and the resin supplies, and all that endless buzzing energy I had... it just vanished. It was like someone just yanked the power cord right out of the wall. 

And when it went, I just... I dropped into this heavy, empty feeling. It's so hard to explain because it wasn't like I was crying because I was upset about the business plan not working out, or because I was mad at my husband anymore. It was just this profound, crushing emptiness. I would go and sit at that exact same kitchen table—the very same one where I was writing out my grand master plans on the back of the grocery receipts just a few days before—and I would just sit there and cry over absolutely nothing. I mean, nothing at all. 

The tears would just fall, and my husband would come into the kitchen and see me, and he'd ask what was wrong, and I couldn't even give him a reason. I didn't have one. I just felt like... like I couldn't get myself back. The woman who was ready to march into Gary's office and quit was gone, but the normal me, the one who just puts on her safety vest and goes to the warehouse and does her job, she was gone too. I was just this heavy shell sitting there, staring at the wood grain on the table, crying into my coffee mug for hours on end. It felt like I was wearing a lead apron, you know, the kind they put over your chest at the dentist for x-rays? Just so heavy. I kept wishing I could figure out how to just be myself again, but I was just stuck in that dark, empty place.
How long did that heavy, empty feeling last after your energy crashed?

Well, honestly, it's still there. That depressed, withdrawn part, that heavy feeling... it's been hanging over me for about three months now. Three whole months. It feels like a lifetime when you're just dragging yourself through every single day, you know? I wake up and I just stare at the bedroom ceiling, listening to my husband getting ready for work, listening to the shower running, and I just think... how on earth am I going to do this? How am I going to put my steel-toe boots on and go pull stock for an entire shift? 

It's been exactly like that ever since that big crash. Just three months of this awful, dark cloud following me into the warehouse, following me down the aisles, following me back home, and sitting right there next to me at the kitchen table. And I try, I really do try to just push through it and be normal, because we have bills to pay. Those electric bills I was writing all my crazy business plans on, they don't stop coming just because I feel completely empty inside. 

But I have to say, even though it's been a solid three months of this, it has become so, so much harder to manage just after these past few weeks. I don't really know what shifted recently, but these last couple of weeks... it's like that lead apron I was telling you about just doubled in weight. I'm finding myself tearing up in the breakroom at work, literally having to hide behind the vending machines so Gary doesn't see me crying and write me up for being off the floor. Three months is just such a long time to feel like a ghost in your own life, but lately, especially these past few weeks, it's just taking every ounce of strength I have left just to pretend I'm okay.
Have you ever had a period of high energy and invincibility like the one you described before this recent episode?

No, never. Honestly, I think that's why it was so... so completely bizarre for both of us. My husband and I, I mean. I have never in my life felt anything even remotely close to that before. 

I've always just been a very steady, predictable person, you know? I mean, I'm forty-eight years old, and I've worked in warehouses for years. Pulling stock, lifting heavy boxes, walking miles and miles on solid concrete floors for eight or ten hours a shift... you don't exactly have boundless energy when you do that for a living. Usually, by the time I get home from my shift, my feet are throbbing, my back aches, and I'm just ready to kick off my steel-toe boots, heat up whatever leftovers we have in the fridge, and watch a little TV before I inevitably fall asleep right there on the living room couch. That's my normal. That's how I've been for as long as I can remember. 

So to suddenly be up all night, buzzing like a refrigerator, feeling like I didn't need to sleep at all, and planning to take over the entire craft world with epoxy resin... it was completely out of left field. My husband was just totally thrown by it. He kept looking at me and asking, "Who are you right now? What has gotten into you?" because in the twenty-odd years we've been together, he has never, ever seen me act like that. 

I've never felt invincible in my entire life. I've always been the practical one, the one worrying about how we're going to pay the electric bill, not the one writing crazy business plans on the back of the envelope it came in. I mean, sure, I've had good days in the past, days where I felt productive and got through my pick list at work faster than usual, and maybe Gary didn't have anything to complain about for once. But that's just normal, everyday stuff. It's not this... this wild, electric, I-can-conquer-the-world feeling where my thoughts are just racing a mile a minute. 

So, no, nothing like that before this past time. This was the very first time anything like that has ever happened to me, and it just... looking back on it now from this awful, heavy place I'm in, it really scares me. It's like I was a completely different person for that week, just some stranger living in my house, using my laptop, ready to throw away my job and my savings. And then she just vanished and left me holding the bag. It makes absolutely no sense to me, it really doesn't. I just don't understand where it came from.
Have you ever felt this heavy, empty feeling before this recent episode?

No... no, I really haven't. Just like that crazy buzzing energy, this heavy, awful feeling is completely new territory for me. 

I mean, don't get me wrong, I've had bad days before. You work on concrete floors for ten hours a day, pulling orders and dealing with a manager like Gary riding you about your pick rates, and you're going to have days where you come home and you just want to cry from sheer exhaustion. There are plenty of nights where my back will ache, my feet will be throbbing, and I might get a little snappy with my husband about, I don't know, leaving his boots in the hallway or something. But that's just normal tired, you know? That's just being forty-eight and working a physical job to make ends meet. You eat dinner, you get some sleep, and you wake up feeling like yourself again. 

It's not... this. I have never, ever felt this kind of crushing emptiness before. Usually, I'm the one holding everything together, making sure the electric bill is paid, making sure we have groceries, just keeping the train on the tracks. If I got stressed in the past, I'd just push through it. I wouldn't just sit there at the kitchen table staring at the wall feeling like there's absolutely nothing left inside of me. I wouldn't be hiding behind vending machines at work to cry over nothing. 

So, no, never. Before this whole nightmare started a few months ago, I had never experienced anything even close to this dark place. It’s like my brain just broke after all that wild energy ran out, and I don't know how to fix it, because I've never had to deal with anything like this in my entire life. I've always been a fighter, you know? A hard worker who just gets the job done. And now I just feel like I'm completely hollowed out, and it's just so terrifying because I don't have any past experience to draw on to figure out how to climb out of it.
Have you ever had any other episodes in your life where you felt extremely energetic, invincible, or unusually confident, similar to what you described happening recently?

Well, like I was saying just a minute ago... no, never before this recent time. This one time, this past episode, was the very first and only time I've ever felt anything like that. But, you know, when I think about that specific week, that time when all this started... it wasn't just that I felt invincible, though I did. I really did. 

At first, I felt so fired up, like I was absolutely unstoppable. I had this whole vision for my epoxy resin craft business, and I was setting up all these new house rules because I just felt so clear-headed and in charge. I felt like I finally had everything figured out, like I was on top of the world and nothing could get in my way. But the thing is, it wasn't all just feeling great and confident. 

Because if my husband even looked at me funny, or if he made the tiniest little comment about what I was doing, or asked why I was still awake at three in the morning... I would just snap at him. And I mean really snap. I'd get so incredibly irritated, like he was purposely trying to hold me back or ruin my plans. He'd just ask a simple question, maybe about the electric bill or why there were craft supplies all over the dining room table, and I would just explode. It was like I had this huge, roaring fire inside me, and he was trying to throw a wet blanket on it, and I just couldn't stand it. 

I've never been like that with him before. We bicker, sure, everyone bickers, especially when you're tired after a long shift at the warehouse, but this was different. This was like my skin was too tight, and any little thing he said that wasn't 100% supportive of my brilliant plans just made me so angry. So, yeah, I felt unstoppable and confident, but I was also just incredibly irritable, snapping at him over the absolute smallest things. But again, that was only during that one specific week recently. Never, ever before in my whole forty-eight years of life. Just that one time.
Did you experience any periods of abnormally elevated or irritable mood that lasted for at least one week?

Yes, exactly, that's what I was just trying to tell you. That one specific week... it was exactly like that. For that whole week, I was just so completely fired up. I mean, I felt almost unstoppable about my new craft business and all these new house rules I was coming up with. I spent days—literally days—reorganizing everything, setting up my epoxy resin stations all over the dining room table, taping schedules and new rules to the refrigerator door because I just knew, I absolutely knew I had finally figured out the perfect way to run our lives. 

But at the exact same time, for that entire week, I was just a live wire. If my husband came into the kitchen and made the smallest comment—like just asking if I was ever going to clear a spot for us to eat, or if I was going to turn the lights off and come to bed—I would just snap at him. I mean, I was vicious. I'd snap over the absolute smallest thing because it felt like he was purposely trying to hold me back. Like I was on the verge of this massive, life-changing success with my business and getting our house in perfect order, and he was just this dead weight trying to ruin my momentum. 

It was a solid seven or eight days of living exactly like that, just bouncing between feeling like I could conquer the universe and wanting to scream at my husband for breathing too loud or looking at my resin molds the wrong way. I'd come home from a long shift at the warehouse—if I even went in, because honestly my mind was a million miles away from pulling pallets—and I'd just immediately start buzzing around the house again, completely wired, and completely ready to bite his head off if he questioned my process. So, yes, it definitely lasted a full week, and it was just... it was exhausting for him, I'm sure, but for me, I just felt so right and so incredibly angry at him at the exact same time.
During that week when you felt invincible and had all the energy, did you need less sleep than usual?

Oh, sleep? Sleep was... honestly, it was like a joke to me that week. I mean, usually, working at the warehouse, by the time I get home, my feet are killing me and I'm practically falling asleep in my dinner plate. But during that week? I think I was sleeping maybe two, sometimes three hours a night. Tops. And the crazy thing is, I wouldn't even wake up tired! You know how normally if you only get a couple of hours of sleep, you feel like you've been hit by a Mack truck the next day? Not me. Not then.

I would lay down at maybe midnight, mostly just because my husband was begging me to come to bed and turn off the overhead lights so he could get some rest, and then by 2:30 or 3:00 in the morning, my eyes would just snap open. And I wasn't just awake, I was completely ready to go. I'd literally pop out of bed, totally wired. I remember looking at the alarm clock, seeing it was 3 AM, and thinking, "Well, I've got a solid three hours before the sun comes up to get these resin molds poured and finish color-coding the new household chore charts." 

It honestly felt like sleep was just this massive waste of time. Like, why would I lay there in the dark with my eyes closed doing absolutely nothing when I had all these brilliant ideas and projects I needed to get done? My husband would come out into the kitchen at 5 AM to get ready for his shift, rubbing his eyes and yawning, and I'd already have the entire dining room table covered in glitter and epoxy, and I'd be talking a mile a minute about my business plan. He'd ask me if I even slept, and I'd just snap at him or brush him off because, to me, sleep was just getting in the way. It was just stealing time that I needed for my projects. I didn't need it, I didn't want it, and my body just completely stopped asking for it. It was like I was running on some kind of super-charged battery that just never, ever ran out of juice.

But to answer what you just asked about whether that ever happened another time in my life for four days or more? No. Absolutely not. Just this one, single episode recently. I can't stress that enough, because it was so incredibly strange and out of character for me to feel that unstoppable and that angry all at once, so I know for a total fact it never happened before. Just this once.
